title: Family First or Everyone Equal?
objective: After this level you can weigh Mozi’s impartial care for all against the Confucian view that love rightly starts with your own family.
summary: The Mohists argued for inclusive care (jian ai) from its consequences and a journey test; Mencius defended care with distinctions that grows outward from the family.

cards.headline: Your nephew or a neighbor’s baby: should you care about them equally?
cards.body: Remember the Mohists from Level 6, who attacked lavish funerals? Their deepest quarrel with the Confucians was about whom to care for.

cards.headline: Inclusive care
cards.body: The Mohists’ best-known teaching is jian ai, usually rendered “inclusive care” or “impartial concern”: care for others without distinguishing self and others, associates and strangers. Their argument ran on consequences. Crime, strife and war come from caring for your own family, city or state and not for others’. If people were for others’ states as for their own, they asked, who would attack another state?

cards.headline: The long journey test
cards.body: The Mohists added a thought experiment. You are leaving on a long journey and must entrust your family to someone. Will you choose a person who cares for everyone impartially, or one who favors their own? Even partial people, the Mohists claimed, would pick the impartial carer.

cards.headline: Love starts at home
cards.body: Confucians held a doctrine of care with distinctions. The Analects calls filial piety the root of goodness, and Mencius taught that benevolence grows by extending the love first shown in the family. He asked the Mohist Yi Zhi whether he truly held that affection for his own nephew is like affection for a neighbor’s baby. Humans naturally care more for relatives, Mencius argued, so a doctrine demanding impartiality is impractical.

cards.headline: Barbs and replies
cards.body: Mencius went further, equating inclusive care with renouncing one’s father and dismissing Mozi as a “beast”. The Mohists replied that impartial concern is no harder than things rulers had already demanded and got from their subjects. Chad Hansen and Bryan Van Norden point to a gap in the journey test: it shows partial people want others to be impartial, not that they should be impartial themselves.

cards.headline: Family First or Everyone Equal?: the big picture
learned: Mohists: inclusive care, argued from consequences

questions.prompt: The Mohists’ teaching jian ai is usually rendered as _____.

options.label: filial piety
options.rationale: That is the Confucian root of goodness.

options.label: non-action
options.rationale: That is the Daoist wu wei.

questions.explanation: Jian ai is usually rendered “inclusive care” or “impartial concern”.

questions.prompt: Match each side or critic with its position.

pairs.right: A gap in the journey test

questions.explanation: The Mohists taught inclusive care, the Confucians held a doctrine of care with distinctions, and Chad Hansen, with Bryan Van Norden, found a gap in the journey test.

questions.prompt: Confucian ren, humaneness, is summed up as “caring for others”. How did Mencius say such benevolence grows?

options.label: By treating strangers exactly as you treat family
options.rationale: That is closer to the Mohist view.

options.label: By extending the love first shown in the family
By following laws and punishments
options.rationale: Mencius looked to human nature, not penalties.

options.label: By withdrawing from society
options.rationale: Mencius wanted benevolence to spread outward.

questions.explanation: Mencius taught that benevolence grows by extending love first shown in the family outward to others.
